steps.prompt: Both start with “after”. What’s different about the first part of each?
steps.b: After we ate lunch, we played tag.
steps.reveal: Both are fine sentences! But look at the first part. “After lunch” has no subject or verb: it’s a phrase. “After we ate lunch” has its own subject and verb (we ate): it’s a clause. Knowing the difference helps you spot fragments and place your commas.

cards.title: Phrase or clause?
cards.body: A phrase is a group of words without its own subject and verb: in the park, running fast, the shiny new bike. A clause has a subject and a verb: the dog barked, because we were late.

cards.title: Independent and dependent
cards.text:
Independent: we were late (a complete thought)
Dependent: because we were late (waits for more)
Together: We missed the bus because we were late.
cards.note: Words like because, when, if, although, after, before, since, until and while make a clause dependent. It can’t be a sentence by itself.

cards.title: Relative clauses
cards.text:
The boy who sits next to me plays the drums.
Our phone, which was brand new, fell in the pool.
The book that I borrowed is overdue.
cards.note: A relative clause starts with who, which or that and describes a noun. Use who for people and which or that for things.

cards.title: The comma rule
cards.telling: When the bell rang we ran outside.
cards.showing: When the bell rang, we ran outside.
cards.note: When a dependent clause comes first, put a comma after it. When it comes last (We ran outside when the bell rang), you usually don’t need one.

prompts: Pick one of your sentences. Which part is the independent clause, and which is dependent?
Why do you think a dependent clause at the start needs a comma?
